Region where patrolling lines in winter is challenging.
article_title: Things to look for in Patrolling
brief_extract:
Trees
growing close to the line must
always be watched, also the
building of hayricks and houses
too near the line.. To patrol the lines in winter in
the North of England is no picnic,
especially as one of our lines, the
Carlisle-Kendal line, passes over
the summit of Shap Fells, at a
height of nearly 1,500 feet above
sea level. Whilst it is very plea-
sant indeed in summer to climb
the summit of Shap and see the
valleys dotted with sheep and the
distant horizon dominated by the
summits of Scafell Pike and the
Langdale Ranges with, far away,
the occasional glimpse of the sea,
in winter, with the temperature
often below freezing point, with
rain and snow, and the peculiar
Helme wind whipping your wet
oilskins round your legs, and
every foot of climb a struggle
against the elements, it is a very
uncomfortable job indeed.

brief_context: An area famous for its pottery and characteristic coal ovens.
brief_extract: Of special interest were the electrically driven automatic making machines and drying stoves and the electrically controlled biscuit and glost continuous ovens which have taken the place of the old coal ovens. These coal ovens, whose familiar shape forms such a feature of the Five Towns, used to take 70/72 hours to heat up to the required temperature, and, after firing, the heat was lost. Now, with the aid of electricity, the correct temperature is obtained and kept constant, and as the trucks containing saggars of unbaked crockery pass down the line, no heat is lost.

brief_context: City mentioned as containing over 80 electrical kilns and ovens.
brief_extract: The ovens operate continuously 24 hours a day throughout the year. brief_context: Origin region of the Stone of Destiny.
brief_extract:
Why he did not
drop it in the depth of the ocean
and put it away for good has
always been a puzzle. But living
in a superstitious age, he may
have had a cautionary awe of its
alleged history — how it had
formed Jacob's pillow when he
dreamt the famous dream of the
ladder reaching up to heaven and
angels ascending and descending,
how it had subsequently travelled
from the East through Spain to
Ireland, and thence to Scone near
Perth to form part of the Scots
coronation chair. At any rate, he
took it away to London, but left
behind the old prophecy :
" The Scots shall brook the realm
as natif ground
If weirds fail not, whair'ere this
stane is found "
remembered by James VI when he
united the crowns, for he rescued
it from its hiding place and made
it part of the Coronation Chair at
Westminster, where it is today.

Sir Walter Scott made Perth
the scene of one of his most fas-
cinating historical novels, which
in turn inspired a great Contin-
ental composer to create an
opera. Sir Walter makes use of
the story of the starvation of the
Duke of Rothesay, who was in-
carcerated in Falkland Castle,
about 15 miles distant from
Perth, and died a horrible death. But no master hand so far has
made use of the equally exciting
story of Rothesay's brother who
became James I—how he came to
Perth with his golden - haired
Queen Joanna and his court to
stay at Blackfriars for Christmas;
how he was stopped at the ferry
by a Highland woman who cried,
"My Lord King, an' ye pass this
water ye shall not turn again
alive." But James was in no mood
to heed the babblings of an old
woman.

article_title: Lighting Ideas from Sweden — Italy — Denmark
brief_extract:
THE ELECTRICAL AGE. APRIL, 1950

Lighting Ideas from
Sweden — Italy — Denmark

THE Scottish Committee of the Council of Industrial Design recently organised an Exhibition of Continental and British lighting fittings to stimulate the industry in Britain and to provide new ideas for interested firms in Scotland. The settings for the sixty table, standard, wall and ceiling fittings suggested every type of room in a modern house or office, and those who have the opportunity of seeing this Exhibition in London in April will recall the words of Professor Gordon Brown, of Edinburgh University, who opened the Exhibition: “ Lighting fittings are related to the rooms in which they are placed, the rooms are related to the house, the house to the street, the street to the town, and the town must be an expression of our national way of life.”

Swedish standard lamp in brass with coloured fabric shade.

article_title: The Borders and the Scott Country
brief_extract: Yet nothing but the beauty of this land of faery and the historic gems it contains could account for the sheer pleasure which the afternoon afforded. This was a gracious countryside with its smiling grassland, its rolling hills, and its clear, broad rivers, so different from the turbulent Highland streams, but the occasional rocky crags and patches of bleak moorland called to mind the battles and the scars which the greensward now covered, and the names both legendary and historical commemorated by the modern sign-posts. As the shadows of the Eildon Hills pursued the party, did they think for a moment that the spirit of "the wondrous wizard Michael Scott" was still abroad, and did they recall the adventure of Thomas the Rhymer who, led by the Queen of Elfland, wandered for seven long years inside these hills where flowed all the blood that ever was shed on earth?

In this enchanted and enchant-
ing country, today and yesterday
are as one, for the party passed
Bemersyde, the seat of the Haigs
for more than 700 years, to tread
the smooth green lawns of Dry-
burgh Abbey ruins where Earl
Haig lies at rest beside an un-
known soldier, each symbolised
by the poppy from Flanders
Fields. Though the spirit of Sir Walter
Scott hovers over the countryside
which he loved so dearly, he too
lies in lovely Dryburgh, while the
intimate reminders of his day-
to-day life are still set out in
stately Abbotsford.

On the Old
Dalkeith Road was the remains
of a tree planted by the Queen of
Scots, and a few yards away was
a sapling planted by the present
Queen Mother. On the banks of the Gala stands
Galashiels, on whose grey build-
ings the sinking sun cast a
mellow glow, and it was here that
tea was so thoughtfully provided,
before the party sped through the
lovely Shire of Peebles, passing
the old Royal Burgh on their re-
turn journey to Edinburgh. The guide was somewhat
amused at the English pronun-
ciation of the small town of
"Penicuik." When asked what
were the hills rising in a grey mist
over Edinburgh, she proudly
answered: "That is Arthur's
seat."

brief_context: Area with extensive peat deposits.
brief_extract: The Irish have turned to advantage their very large-scale peat deposits, for they have no coal. Over 2,000 square miles of the north of Scotland is under a blanket of peat, and a great deal of the agricultural land was slowly won in the past centuries by stripping off the layer of peat. It is now proposed to do this on a much greater scale, and research is being carried out in Scotland to determine how best to dry the peat economically, destroy it and turn it into power, in power stations near the bogs.

World Energy Sources

A Conference of engineers may not at first sight appear to have much immediate significance for the home, but when we learn that in many countries a date can be fixed when all available resources for the production of energy will be used up, then we realise how much we are affected by the matters discussed. For instance, in Great Britain our coal reserves are estimated to last for some further centuries. The possible water power resources have been surveyed, and the major ones are being developed, but the increasing demand for electricity means intensive research to discover and exploit hitherto untapped sources of energy.

brief_context: The source of steel plate used in the factory.
brief_extract: THE Pressed Steel Company’s factory at Oxford is one of the largest in Europe. Here, from gigantic rolls of steel plate, much of it from South Wales, pressings for every part of a car body and several types of refrigerator cabinet are made simultaneously.
